title: sync.Once & sync.Map
summary: `sync.Once` guarantees a piece of code runs **exactly once**, no matter how many goroutines call it — the idiomatic way to do lazy, thread-safe initialization. `sync.Map` is a specialized concurrent map optimized for a narrow set of access patterns. Both exist to solve concurrency problems that a plain mutex handles clumsily.

subtopics.title: once.Do runs exactly once
subtopics.explanation: A sync.Once has a single method, Do(f). The first goroutine to call Do runs f; every other goroutine blocks until f returns, then all of them skip it. Even on later calls, f never runs again. The zero value is ready to use — never copy a Once after first use.
subtopics.example:
var once sync.Once
once.Do(setup) // setup runs once, ever

subtopics.title: The happens-before guarantee
subtopics.explanation: once.Do doesn't just prevent re-running f — it also establishes a memory barrier. Whatever f writes is guaranteed visible to every goroutine that returns from Do. That's why lazy singletons built on Once are safe to read without further locking.
subtopics.example:
once.Do(func(){ cfg = load() })
use(cfg) // cfg fully published

subtopics.title: Once and panics
subtopics.explanation: If f panics, Once still considers Do 'done' — f will not be retried on a later call. If you need retry-on-failure, you must build it yourself (e.g. with a mutex and a success flag), because Once deliberately offers no retry.
subtopics.example: once.Do(mayPanic) // a later Do is a no-op even after panic

subtopics.title: What sync.Map is for
subtopics.explanation: sync.Map is a concurrent map optimized for two cases: (1) a key is written once and read many times, or (2) goroutines operate on disjoint sets of keys. In those cases it can beat a map guarded by sync.RWMutex. For general read-write workloads, a plain map + RWMutex is usually faster and clearer.
subtopics.example:
var m sync.Map
m.Store("k", 1)
v, ok := m.Load("k")

subtopics.title: LoadOrStore & atomic upserts
subtopics.explanation: sync.Map exposes Load, Store, Delete, LoadOrStore, LoadAndDelete, and Range. LoadOrStore atomically returns an existing value or stores and returns a new one — perfect for building a one-instance-per-key cache without a separate lock. Range does not give a consistent snapshot; entries may be added or removed during iteration.

subtopics.title: sync.Map is not generic and untyped
subtopics.explanation: sync.Map stores keys and values as interface{} (any), so you lose static typing and pay boxing costs. For a typed, simpler concurrent map you often wrap a plain map[K]V with a sync.RWMutex, which is also easier to reason about.
subtopics.example:
v, ok := m.Load(k)
n := v.(int) // type assertion needed

foundations.overview: Concurrent code frequently needs two things: to initialize something exactly once even when many goroutines race to do it, and to share a map across goroutines safely. Go's sync package provides purpose-built tools for both. sync.Once turns 'lazy, thread-safe init' from a tricky double-checked-locking puzzle into a single method call. sync.Map is a concurrent map tuned for specific access patterns where a plain mutex-guarded map would contend. Knowing when each helps — and when a plain mutex is better — is the mark of an engineer who understands Go concurrency rather than just memorizing primitives.
foundations.formalDefinition: sync.Once is an object that performs an action at most once; its Do method calls the passed function only on the first invocation and blocks concurrent callers until it returns, establishing a happens-before edge from the function's body to all callers. sync.Map is a concurrent map safe for use by multiple goroutines without external locking, optimized for write-once-read-many and disjoint-key-set workloads.
foundations.whyItMatters: Lazy initialization races are a classic source of subtle, hard-to-reproduce bugs; sync.Once removes that whole bug class in one line. sync.Map appears constantly in interviews as a 'when would you use this instead of a mutex?' probe, and choosing the wrong concurrent-map strategy directly affects throughput under load.
foundations.mentalModel: Think of sync.Once as a turnstile with a one-shot latch: the first person through pulls the lever (runs f); everyone else waits at the gate until the lever finishes, then walks through freely forever after — the lever never moves again. Think of sync.Map as a coat-check designed for a venue where most patrons drop a coat once and pick it up later (write-once, read-many), not a busy locker room with constant swaps.
foundations.runtimePerspective: Internally sync.Once holds a done flag (read with an atomic load on the fast path) plus a mutex used only on the first, slow path. After the first call, Do is a cheap atomic check with no locking. sync.Map keeps two internal maps — a mostly-read-only atomic map for the fast path and a 'dirty' map guarded by a mutex for writes — and promotes the dirty map to read-only after enough misses, which is what amortizes its cost for read-heavy workloads.
foundations.realWorldUsage: sync.Once backs lazy singletons: a database pool, a parsed config, a compiled regexp, a metrics registry. sync.Map appears in connection caches, per-key rate limiters, and registries where many goroutines look up by distinct keys.
foundations.businessImpact: Correct one-time initialization avoids duplicate expensive setup (opening two DB pools, double-charging a startup cost) and the outages that race conditions cause. Picking the right concurrent-map strategy keeps p99 latency low under load, protecting user experience and infra cost.
foundations.engineeringImpact: sync.Once replaces error-prone hand-rolled double-checked locking, so teams write less fragile concurrency code. Understanding sync.Map's niche prevents cargo-culting it everywhere and the performance regressions that follow.
foundations.performanceImpact: After the first call, once.Do is a single atomic load — effectively free on the hot path. sync.Map shines for read-mostly or disjoint-key access but can be slower and allocate more than a plain map + RWMutex for mixed read/write workloads, so benchmark before adopting it.
commonUseCases: Lazy singletons (DB pool, config, logger) via sync.Once
Compiling an expensive resource (regexp, template) exactly once
Concurrent caches keyed by id using sync.Map.LoadOrStore
Per-key registries where goroutines touch disjoint keys

commonMisconceptions.myth: sync.Once retries the function if it fails or panics.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Once marks itself done as soon as Do returns, even via panic. The function will never run again; build your own retry if you need it.

commonMisconceptions.myth: sync.Map is just a faster map you should always reach for.
commonMisconceptions.reality: It's optimized for write-once-read-many and disjoint keys. For general mixed workloads a plain map guarded by sync.RWMutex is usually faster and clearer.

commonMisconceptions.myth: You must lock around once.Do or pass a pointer.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Do is internally synchronized; you call it directly. You must not copy the Once value after first use, though.

visualExplorer.title: How once.Do serializes initialization
visualExplorer.caption: Many goroutines call Do at the same time; exactly one runs f while the rest wait, then everyone proceeds.

config.intro: Three goroutines race to call once.Do(load). Here is what the runtime does:

steps.name: Fast-path check
steps.detail: Each caller atomically reads the `done` flag. If it's already set, Do returns immediately with no locking.

steps.name: First caller wins the lock
steps.detail: On the first call done is 0, so callers take an internal mutex. The first one in begins running f; the others block on the mutex.

steps.name: f runs exactly once
steps.detail: Only the winning goroutine executes load(). Its writes (e.g. assigning the singleton) happen here.

steps.name: Set done & publish
steps.detail: After f returns, Do atomically sets done=1. This establishes happens-before: f's writes are now visible to all callers.

steps.name: Everyone proceeds
steps.detail: Waiting goroutines wake, see done=1, skip f, and return. Every future Do call hits the fast path and skips f forever.

interactiveExamples.title: A thread-safe lazy singleton with sync.Once
interactiveExamples.explanation: Even though three goroutines race to call instance(), the expensive setup runs exactly once and every caller gets the same pointer. once.Do also publishes the write to `db` safely.

interactiveExamples.title: Edit it: build a per-key cache with sync.Map
interactiveExamples.explanation: We want getConn(key) to create at most one connection per key, even under concurrency. Replace the racy plain-map logic with sync.Map.LoadOrStore so the creation is atomic per key.

checkpoints.explanation: once.Do runs its function only on the first call. The next two Do calls see the done flag set and skip the function entirely, so 'init' prints once, then 'done'.

checkpoints.prompt: When is sync.Map the better choice over a map guarded by sync.RWMutex?
options: When keys are written once and read many times, or goroutines use disjoint key sets
Only for maps with fewer than 10 keys
When you need a consistent snapshot during iteration
checkpoints.explanation: sync.Map is optimized for write-once-read-many and disjoint-key workloads. For general mixed read/write traffic a plain map + RWMutex is usually faster, and sync.Map's Range gives no consistent snapshot.

checkpoints.prompt: This code wants to retry initialization if it fails. What's wrong?
options: After the first call, Do never runs f again — a failed init is never retried, and err is nil on later calls
checkpoints.explanation: Once marks itself done as soon as Do returns, even if connect() failed. Later setup() calls skip the function, so err is the zero value (nil) and the failed initialization is never retried. Use a mutex + success flag if you need retry semantics.

checkpoints.prompt: Complete the call so the value is created at most once per key under concurrency.
checkpoints.explanation: LoadOrStore atomically returns the existing value (loaded=true) or stores and returns the new one (loaded=false). Store always overwrites, and Load can't create. Note: newConn() is still evaluated eagerly here even if a value already exists.

codeLab.title: A lazy, thread-safe counter singleton
codeLab.instructions: Implement `Get() *Counter` that returns a single shared *Counter, initialized lazily and exactly once even when many goroutines call Get concurrently. Counter has an Inc() method that is itself goroutine-safe.
hints: Inside Get, call once.Do with a function that assigns instance = &Counter{}.
Return instance after Do — once.Do guarantees the write is visible to every caller.

debuggingLab.title: Initialization runs more than once
debuggingLab.symptom: The 'init' message prints multiple times even though sync.Once is used, and `go vet` complains about copying a lock.
debuggingLab.errorAnalysis: Setup has a value receiver, so each call operates on a fresh COPY of Service — including a freshly-zeroed sync.Once whose done flag is false. The 'once' is therefore brand new every call, so Do runs again. sync.Once must never be copied after use; go vet's copylocks check flags this.
commonMistakes: Using a value receiver on a method that calls a sync primitive's method.
Storing sync.Once (or Mutex) by value and then copying the struct.
debuggingLab.fixChallenge: Use a pointer receiver so all calls share the same Once.

theory.question: What guarantees does sync.Once provide beyond 'run once'?
theory.directAnswer: Two guarantees. First, the function passed to Do runs at most once across all goroutines; concurrent callers block until the first call returns. Second, it establishes a happens-before relationship: any memory written inside the function is guaranteed visible to every goroutine that returns from Do, so a singleton initialized inside Do can be read safely without further synchronization.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A one-shot synchronization primitive with a single Do method.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: To replace error-prone double-checked locking for lazy, thread-safe initialization.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: A fast-path atomic check of a done flag, and on the first call only, an internal mutex that serializes callers; after f returns, done is set with release semantics that publish f's writes.

theory.whyImportant: The memory-visibility guarantee is what makes lazy singletons correct; candidates who only say 'runs once' miss half the value.
theory.realWorldExample: A package-level GetLogger() uses once.Do to build the logger lazily; callers across many goroutines safely read the fully-constructed logger.

followUps.question: What happens if the function passed to Do panics?
followUps.answer: Once still considers itself done, so a later Do is a no-op. The function will not be retried; for retry-on-failure you must roll your own with a mutex and a success flag.

followUps.question: Can you reset a sync.Once?
followUps.answer: No public reset exists. You'd assign a new Once value to the variable, which is only safe if no goroutine is using it concurrently.

theory.question: When would you use sync.Map instead of a map protected by sync.RWMutex?
theory.directAnswer: Use sync.Map when access fits its two optimized cases: a key is written once then read many times, or different goroutines mostly touch disjoint sets of keys. In those workloads its internal read-only/dirty-map split reduces lock contention. For general mixed read/write traffic, a plain map + sync.RWMutex is usually faster, type-safe, and easier to reason about.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A concurrent map in the sync package safe for multi-goroutine use without external locks.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: To optimize specific concurrent access patterns where a single mutex would contend heavily.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: It keeps a mostly-immutable read map served via atomics and a mutex-guarded dirty map for writes, promoting dirty to read after enough read misses to amortize cost.

theory.whyImportant: Reaching for sync.Map by default is a common mistake that can regress performance; knowing its niche shows real concurrency judgment.
theory.realWorldExample: A connection registry keyed by remote address, where each address is established once and read on every subsequent request, is a natural fit for sync.Map.LoadOrStore.

followUps.question: Why is sync.Map untyped?
followUps.answer: Its keys and values are stored as `any` (interface{}), predating generics, so you pay boxing costs and need type assertions on read.

followUps.question: Does Range give a consistent snapshot?
followUps.answer: No. Range visits each key at most once but entries may be added or deleted concurrently, so it reflects no single point-in-time view.

scenario.question: A service opens its database pool inside a sync.Once. Sometimes the very first connect fails (DB still booting), and from then on every request gets a nil pool. How do you fix this?
scenario.directAnswer: The bug is that sync.Once marks itself done even when the function fails, so the failed init is never retried and the pool stays nil. sync.Once is the wrong tool when initialization can fail and should be retried. Replace it with a mutex plus a 'ready' flag: lock, check the flag, attempt connect, set the flag only on success; on failure leave it false so the next caller retries. Alternatively initialize eagerly at startup and fail fast.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A misuse of Once for fallible initialization.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Once is intentionally retry-free; it can't distinguish success from failure.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Do sets done as soon as the function returns, including after an error or panic, so subsequent calls skip it.

scenario.whyImportant: Lazy init that can fail is extremely common (databases, remote configs); using Once there causes hard-down outages.
scenario.realWorldExample: A pod starts before its database is reachable; the first request triggers a failed connect, and Once permanently caches the failure until the pod restarts.

followUps.question: Sketch the retrying initializer.
followUps.answer: Hold a mutex and a bool; in get(): lock, if !ready { if err := connect(); err == nil { ready = true } else { unlock; return err } }, unlock, return the pool. Each failed call leaves ready false so the next retries.

coding.question: Implement a generic, concurrency-safe memoizer `Once[T]` that computes a value lazily exactly once and caches it. Provide `func (o *Once[T]) Do(f func() T) T`.
coding.thoughtProcess: This is sync.Once with a return value. Wrap a sync.Once: on the first Do, run f and store its result in a field; on every call, return the stored field. Because once.Do publishes the write, later reads of the field are safe. Generics give us type safety without boxing.
coding.lineByLine: Once[T] embeds a sync.Once and a typed slot val. Do delegates to once.Do, which guarantees f runs at most once; we assign its result to o.val inside the function. Every caller then returns o.val — safe to read without extra locking because once.Do's completion happens-before every Do return. Generics avoid the interface{} boxing that the standard sync.Map would impose.
coding.timeComplexity: O(cost of f) on the first call; O(1) thereafter.
coding.spaceComplexity: O(1) extra plus the size of T.

followUps.question: Why use a pointer receiver?
followUps.answer: sync.Once must not be copied after use; a value receiver would copy it on each call, breaking the once semantics and tripping go vet's copylocks check.

followUps.question: How would you support error returns with retry?
followUps.answer: Drop sync.Once and use a mutex with a done flag: only set done when f returns a nil error, otherwise leave it false so the next Do retries.

productionDeepDive.architecture: Expose lazy resources through a single accessor (e.g. instance()) backed by sync.Once so callers never touch the raw global. For fallible init, prefer eager startup initialization with fail-fast, or a mutex+flag retrying initializer — never Once.
productionDeepDive.performance: once.Do is a single atomic load on the hot path, so guarding hot reads with it is essentially free. Benchmark sync.Map against map+RWMutex for your real access pattern; sync.Map's read-only/dirty promotion only pays off for read-mostly or disjoint-key traffic.
productionDeepDive.concurrency: Never copy a sync.Once or sync.Map after first use; pass them by pointer and embed by value in a struct accessed via pointer receivers. Run tests with -race to catch accidental shared-map writes.
productionDeepDive.reliability: Because Once caches failures, fallible lazy init can wedge a process into a permanent bad state until restart. Add health checks and prefer retrying initializers for anything that talks to the network.
productionDeepDive.observability: Emit a metric or log the first time a Once-guarded resource initializes so you can correlate cold-start latency. For sync.Map-backed caches, export size and hit/miss counters.
productionDeepDive.security: Ensure secrets loaded inside a Once are not logged in the init function, and that a failed-and-cached init can't silently fall back to an insecure default.

caseStudies.problem: Compiling a regexp or template on every request is wasteful.
caseStudies.solution: Compile once into a package-level var (often via sync.Once or package init).
caseStudies.tradeoffs: Slight cold-start cost vs. amortized speed; must handle compile errors at init.
caseStudies.lessons: One-time compilation behind a single accessor is the idiomatic Go pattern.

caseStudies.problem: A mutex-guarded map became a contention hotspot under read-heavy load.
caseStudies.solution: Switched read-mostly registries to sync.Map after benchmarking.
caseStudies.tradeoffs: Lost static typing and added type assertions for lower contention.
caseStudies.lessons: Measure first — sync.Map helps only for its specific patterns, not as a blanket replacement.

keyTakeaways: sync.Once runs its function at most once across all goroutines and publishes that function's writes to every caller (a happens-before guarantee), making it the idiomatic lazy-singleton tool.
Once marks itself done even if the function panics or fails — it never retries, so don't use it for fallible initialization that should be retried.
sync.Map is specialized for write-once-read-many and disjoint-key workloads; for general mixed read/write, a plain map + sync.RWMutex is usually faster and type-safe.
Never copy a sync.Once or sync.Map after use; access them through pointers, and reach for sync.Map only after benchmarking your actual access pattern.
